Chapter 6: The Illusion of Progress—When Growth Leaves People Behind.
Picture this: a city skyline filled with cranes, new towers going up where older buildings once stood. Billboards everywhere promise a brighter tomorrow—faster internet, smarter homes, opportunities that seem endless. But if you really look, you’ll notice faces pressed to the glass, watching all this change unfold without them. For every story of someone making it big, there’s another story—someone quietly left behind, asking themselves, “When did progress stop including people like me?”
The world we live in—what some call McWorld—is built on the idea that growth is always good. More products, more choices, more ways to connect. In theory, all this should lift everyone up. But in reality, the benefits usually flow to those who are already ahead of the game. Think about a small business owner, suddenly struggling because a global chain moves in and cuts prices she can’t match. Or that factory worker who loses his job to automation—he’s told to “retrain” for a future that feels too far out of reach. Suddenly, the promise of progress starts to sound pretty empty.
Most people don’t notice this gap until it gets wide enough to fall through. Sure, there are new stores and shiny gadgets, but there are also empty storefronts and neighbors quietly moving away. That sense of community—the thing that made a neighborhood feel like home—starts to unravel. It hits you: growth, when it’s driven only by the market, can be a double-edged sword. It creates wealth for some, but leaves many others feeling insecure.
Over time, a quiet frustration builds up. People are told to adapt, to keep up, to embrace whatever’s new. But not everyone can, and let’s be honest—not everyone wants to. The skills and traditions that once mattered are labeled “outdated.” The world moves on, but not everyone comes along for the ride.
And in this new landscape, searching for meaning becomes urgent. People want more than just the next new thing—they want to feel valued. They want to know their work, their lives, actually matter. When progress feels like something that happens to you, not with you, resentment naturally grows. The dream of a better future fades, replaced by nostalgia for a past that, for all its flaws, at least felt like home.
The illusion of progress is strong, but it can’t hide the truth: not everyone’s been invited to the party. The real challenge? Finding a way forward that welcomes everyone—not just those who fit the mold of the global consumer. Until then, the promise of McWorld will stay just that—a promise, not a reality.
